summary: This standards-track memo defines RSVP-TE extensions for creating backup label-switched paths, which protect LSP tunnels by allowing local repair. Traffic can be redirected in tens of milliseconds after a failure. It defines two methods, one-to-one and facility backup.

plainLanguage.summary: A long-distance highway normally carries this tunnel's traffic. If a bridge on that highway collapses, calling the traffic manager at the far end, discussing a new route and then driving it is far too slow for a live phone call. RFC 4090 has the network build detours before anything breaks. The driver right at the bridge switches to the detour the moment the bridge fails, in a fraction of a second, and the traffic manager only re-plans the whole route later, at leisure.

questions: difference between one-to-one and facility backup
what is a point of local repair
what is the rsvp detour object
subtitle: How pre-computed backup tunnels let a router next to a failure switch traffic in 10s of milliseconds, before the head-end even knows something broke.

tldr.problem: When a link or router fails on an MPLS traffic-engineered tunnel, waiting for failure signals to reach the head-end and for a new path to be computed and signaled takes far longer than real-time traffic such as voice over IP can tolerate.
tldr.mechanism: Backup label-switched paths are computed and signaled in advance of any failure. The router next to the failure, the point of local repair (PLR), switches traffic onto the backup locally. Two methods are defined: one-to-one backup, which signals a separate detour LSP for each protected LSP, and facility backup, which builds one bypass tunnel that many LSPs can share. New FAST_REROUTE and DETOUR objects in RSVP carry the instructions.
tldr.outcome: Redirection happens within 10s of milliseconds because no path computation and no signaling are needed after the failure. The RFC is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 8271, RFC 8537, RFC 8796 and RFC 9705.

today: RFC 4090 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2005. It has been updated by RFC 8271, RFC 8537, RFC 8796 and RFC 9705, and no RFC obsoletes it. Read those updates alongside this text when implementing.

sections.title: What This RFC Does
sections.content:
RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) sets up label-switched path (LSP) tunnels along an explicit route. When a link or router on that route fails, ordinary RSVP-TE has to notice the failure, signal the error to the head-end, compute a new path and signal it. RFC 4090 extends RSVP-TE so that backup LSP tunnels exist before any failure occurs, and the router closest to the damage, the point of local repair (PLR), redirects traffic onto the backup itself. The RFC calls this local repair.

The extensions apply only to explicitly routed LSPs. LSPs that change their route dynamically, such as those used in unicast IGP routing, are out of scope. The head-end asks for protection by setting flags in the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object and may optionally include a FAST_REROUTE object that specifies the priorities, bandwidth and attribute filters the backup must use.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC teaches an MPLS tunnel how to carry a spare route with it, ready for the router next to any break to switch over at once.

sections.title: Why Tens of Milliseconds Matter
sections.content:
Real-time applications such as voice over IP need user traffic redirected onto backup tunnels in 10s of milliseconds. That timing can only be met if two slow parts are removed from the recovery: path computation and signaling. The RFC meets this by computing and signaling backup tunnels in advance of failure, and by redirecting traffic as close to the failure point as possible. Because the PLR sits beside the failed link or node, redirection includes no failure-notification delay across the network and no new path setup.

Speed of repair is the primary advantage of the methods described here. The head-end still plays its part: when it learns of the failure it can reoptimize the tunnel along a better long-term path, possibly using a Path Computation Element for inter-area routes. The locally repaired path is treated as temporary.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone call breaks up if the network takes a second to recover. So the fix has to be local and already prepared: no waiting for messages from far away, no fresh route calculation after the break.

sections.title: One-to-One Detours and Facility Bypass Tunnels
sections.content:
A protected LSP is an explicitly routed LSP that has been given protection. Protection comes in two methods.

One-to-one backup: the PLR creates a separate backup LSP, called a detour LSP, for each protected LSP that passes through it. The detour begins at the PLR and merges back into the protected LSP at a merge point (MP) downstream. Detours can be signaled with the sender template-specific method, which gives each detour its own SENDER_TEMPLATE and identifies it with a DETOUR object, or the path-specific method, which keeps the same SESSION and SENDER_TEMPLATE and relies on routers to merge paths.

Facility backup: the PLR builds one bypass tunnel that starts at the PLR, avoids the protected link or node and ends at a merge point. Many protected LSPs that share the same risk can all use that single bypass tunnel. At the PLR their labels are stacked on top of the bypass tunnel's label, so the shared tunnel works like a bypass lane under the main road.

Both methods can protect a single link (the PLR is the upstream router of the failed link) or a whole node (the backup avoids the next router entirely; the flag 'node protection desired' asks for this). The RFC requires that routers on protected paths assume they may be merge points, even if only the PLR knows it.
sections.plainLanguage: One method gives every protected tunnel its own private detour. The other builds one shared bypass around the danger zone that many tunnels can use at once. Both can dodge just the road, or the road and the junction.

sections.title: FAST_REROUTE, DETOUR and the Flags That Ask for Protection
sections.content:
The FAST_REROUTE object (Class-Num 205, C-Type 1) is inserted into the PATH message only by the head-end and must not be changed downstream. It carries the Setup Priority and Hold Priority of the backup (0 to 7, where 0 is highest), a Hop-limit bounding how many extra hops the backup may take from PLR to MP, Flags, a Bandwidth value as a 32-bit IEEE floating point in bytes per second, and the Include-any, Exclude-any and Include-all 32-bit attribute filter vectors. In the Flags field, 0x01 requests the one-to-one backup method and 0x02 requests facility backup. C-Type 7 is a pre-standard format still used by legacy implementations and is reserved; it has a Reserved byte where Flags sits and omits Include-all.

The DETOUR object (Class-Num 63) identifies detour LSPs in the one-to-one, sender template-specific method. C-Type 7 holds IPv4 pairs of PLR_ID and Avoid_Node_ID; C-Type 8 holds the same for IPv6 (128-bit addresses). A DETOUR object may carry several pairs, one for each PLR whose detour has merged; Avoid_Node_ID names the immediate downstream node the PLR is avoiding and is mandatory for the merge rules. The high-order bit of the Class-Num is zero, so routers that do not understand DETOUR must reject the PATH message with a PathErr rather than silently forwarding it.

The SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object gains two flags: bandwidth protection desired (0x08) and node protection desired (0x10). Existing flags still apply: local protection desired (0x01) permits local repair, label recording desired (0x02) asks routers to include labels in the Record Route Object, and SE Style desired (0x04) lets the head-end reroute without tearing the tunnel down. In the RRO address sub-objects, four flags report the outcome: local protection available (0x01), local protection in use (0x02), bandwidth protection (0x04) and node protection (0x08). A PLR that could only protect the link, not the node, sets local protection available but must leave node protection cleared.
sections.plainLanguage: The head-end writes an order form on the tunnel: which kind of backup, how much bandwidth to reserve, how far the detour may wander. Extra tags in the path record tell everyone later whether a detour exists, whether traffic is on it right now, and whether it really covers the bandwidth and the next router.

sections.title: Head-End and PLR Behavior
sections.content:
The head-end requests protection in the PATH message and, over time, watches the RRO flags to learn what it got. When the head-end learns of a failure it may reoptimize the protected LSP along a different, more optimal path; in the global revertive mode this decision is made at the head-end, and the RFC says the global mode SHOULD always be used. An optional local revertive mode lets the PLR try to move traffic back onto the restored resource itself, which matters when the head-end cannot reroute, for example when paths are pinned by an offline optimization tool. If a PLR is configured for local revertive mode but the MP is not, the PLR's attempt to resignal over the restored resource fails, and traffic simply stays on the backup until the head-end reoptimizes.

At the PLR, protection works like this. The PLR selects a backup path for each protected LSP, subject to the FAST_REROUTE object's priorities, hop-limit, bandwidth and filters, and signals it ahead of time. PathTear messages for the protected LSP must also propagate to the detour, but when a PLR receives ResvTear or PathErr messages from downstream for a protected LSP, it must not pass them upstream as long as a detour is up. When the PLR detects a failure on the protected LSP it MUST rapidly switch packets to the backup LSP instead of the normal out-segment, with the stated goal of completing redirection within 10s of milliseconds. In the facility method, after switching, the PLR keeps refreshing the protected LSP's state through the bypass tunnel so downstream routers see no change.
sections.plainLanguage: The head-end places the order and later re-plans the route when it hears about the damage. The router at the break does the instant work: it already holds a ready alternative and flips traffic onto it the moment the next link goes dark.

sections.title: Merge Points and Everyone Else's Job
sections.content:
A router is a merge point when it receives the PATH message of a protected LSP and one or more backup LSPs that merge back into it. In the one-to-one method the LSR knows before failure; in the facility method it may first learn of the role when a backup PATH arrives after a failure, so every LSR on a protected path SHOULD always assume it is a merge point. Reception of a backup PATH before failure does not mean a failure has happened.

With the sender template-specific method, a merge point may see PATH messages with different SENDER_TEMPLATEs for the protected LSP and several detours. Those sharing an outgoing interface and next hop, with the same ERO from the merge point onward, are eligible to merge; the final forwarded PATH must be that of the protected LSP. With the path-specific method, PATH messages with identical SESSION and SENDER_TEMPLATE arrive on different interfaces and MUST be merged: the protected LSP wins if present; otherwise detours that traverse nodes other detours want to avoid are eliminated, and if nothing remains the MP may compute a fresh route avoiding all avoided nodes. Merged detours reserve bandwidth only once, for the final Path. The DETOUR object of the outgoing message combines all merged (PLR_ID, Avoid_Node_ID) pairs.

On a downstream link failure, routers MUST NOT immediately clear Path and Resv state or send PathTear and ResvErr; they SHOULD reset refresh timers to give the PLR time to start refreshing through the backup, with state removed only if not refreshed before the timer expires. Every LSR in the traffic-engineered network should support the DETOUR object and detour merging; LSRs that do not can be avoided by excluding a link attribute from backup paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The merge point is where the detour rejoins the main route. It quietly folds the detours back in, and when a link fails it waits, keeping the old state alive, so the switching router upstream has time to take over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC introduces no new security issues beyond those of RSVP itself (RFC 2205), whose security considerations remain relevant. It does note one specific trust relationship: the facility backup method requires that a PLR and its selected merge point trust the RSVP messages they receive from each other, because after a failure the PLR begins refreshing protected LSP state through the bypass tunnel on behalf of the original head-end.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol adds no new attacks of its own, but the two routers on either side of a shared bypass must trust each other's routing messages, because one will speak for the other after a failure.

left.title: One-to-One Backup
left.desc: A separate detour LSP per protected LSP, from the PLR to a merge point. Identified by the DETOUR object in the sender template-specific method.

right.title: Facility Backup
right.desc: One shared bypass tunnel around the failed link or node; many protected LSPs stack their labels on it at the PLR.

fields.name: Setup Priority
fields.desc: Priority for taking resources, 0 to 7, 0 highest; used when deciding whether this backup may preempt another session.

fields.name: Hold Priority
fields.desc: Priority for holding resources, 0 to 7, 0 highest.

fields.name: Hop-limit
fields.desc: Maximum extra hops the backup path may take from PLR to MP, excluding the PLR and MP themselves; 0 means only direct links.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: 0x01 One-to-One Backup Desired; 0x02 Facility Backup Desired. Inserted only by the head-end LER.

fields.name: Bandwidth
fields.desc: Bandwidth estimate; 32-bit IEEE floating point in bytes per second.

fields.name: Include-any
fields.desc: 32-bit attribute filter vector; any listed attribute makes a link acceptable.

fields.name: Exclude-any
fields.desc: 32-bit attribute filter vector; any listed attribute rules a link out.

fields.name: Include-all
fields.desc: 32-bit attribute filter vector; all listed attributes must be present. Omitted in the legacy C-Type 7 format.

viz.caption: REQUEST AND REPORT FLAGS (RFC 4090, SECTIONS 4.3 AND 4.4)

items.label: Local protection desired (SESSION_ATTRIBUTE)
items.desc: Permits transit routers to use a local repair mechanism, which may violate the explicit route.

items.label: SE Style desired (SESSION_ATTRIBUTE)
items.desc: Lets the head-end reroute without tearing the tunnel down; SHOULD be set when requesting fast reroute.

items.label: Bandwidth protection desired (SESSION_ATTRIBUTE)
items.desc: Asks PLRs for a backup path with a bandwidth guarantee, either the FAST_REROUTE object's value or the protected LSP's bandwidth.

items.label: Node protection desired (SESSION_ATTRIBUTE)
items.desc: Asks PLRs for a backup that bypasses at least the next node, not just the next link.

items.label: Local protection available / in use (RRO)
items.desc: Reports that a local repair mechanism exists for the next hop, and that traffic is on it right now.

items.label: Bandwidth protection / node protection (RRO)
items.desc: Reports that the backup guarantees the requested bandwidth, or that it also survives failure of the next router.

viz.caption: PROTECTION BEFORE AND AFTER FAILURE (RFC 4090, SECTIONS 3 AND 6.3.3)

messages.label: PATH: protected LSP with local protection desired
messages.note: The head-end may also include a FAST_REROUTE object naming priorities, hop-limit and bandwidth.

messages.label: PATH: backup detour or bypass tunnel, pre-signaled
messages.note: Set up before any failure; in the one-to-one sender template-specific method this PATH carries a DETOUR object.

messages.label: Link or node failure detected; traffic switched onto backup
messages.note: The PLR MUST rapidly switch packets; the goal is redirection within 10s of milliseconds.

messages.label: Later: reoptimize the protected LSP (global revertive mode)
messages.note: Once the head-end learns of the failure, it may compute a better long-term path.
